lines: A real piece of work can report that it isn't ready yet, several times in a row, before it finally says yes.
If a caller goes ahead and does the work anyway, while it's still saying not ready, what's actually allowed to happen?
answer: Doing the work before a genuine yes is not a minor shortcut; it breaks the whole agreement.

lines: Run it for real: the piece of work said not ready several times in a row,
and only once it had genuinely become ready did a caller actually go ahead and do the work.

Wrap that same kind of work in four different wrappers at once: one that caps how many run together, one that turns work away immediately, one that spaces work out over time, and one that gives up past a deadline.
Send a whole batch of work through all four together. How many of those four actually change what happens to that batch, rather than just watching it pass by?
answer: Each one bounds a genuinely different thing about that batch.

lines: Run it for real: the cap genuinely limited how many ran at once, the turn-away wrapper genuinely rejected one immediately instead of waiting,
the spacing wrapper genuinely stretched the work out over real time, and the deadline wrapper genuinely gave up on work that ran too long.
steps.takeaway: A wrapper sits around one piece of work without touching its own code, and each wrapper bounds a different real thing.

lines: Put a queue in front of a piece of work whose own concurrency is capped at just one, then send several requests in all at once.
Does that queue turn away the extra requests, the same way the turn-away wrapper did?
answer: It accepts every one of them up front into its own queue, no matter what the work underneath can actually get through.

lines: Run it for real: the queue accepted every request immediately,
while the work hiding behind it still only ran one at a time underneath — a real, hidden backlog, not a rejection.
steps.takeaway: A queue in front of a piece of work can quietly hide the very backlog a hard cap exists to prevent, unless it's sized on purpose.

lines: Go back to the very first question: a caller goes ahead and does the work without ever checking whether it's ready first.
What does the documentation for this agreement actually say is allowed to happen?
answer: That's not a side effect; it's exactly what the documentation itself permits.

lines: The documentation's own words settle it directly: an implementation is allowed to break outright,
if work arrives before it has genuinely reported that it's ready.
Asking if something is ready, and asking it to actually do the work, are two separate steps on purpose.
That split is the whole agreement about overload, and every wrapper placed around a piece of work composes around that exact same agreement.
steps.takeaway: Readiness isn't a formality bolted on afterward; it's the whole agreement about overload, and every wrapper composes around that same agreement.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: a real piece of work that says not ready, and a caller that genuinely waits for a real yes before doing the work.
Four separate wrappers, each one bounding a different real thing about a batch of work.
A queue that can accept work the thing underneath it cannot yet get through, a real hidden backlog unless it's sized on purpose.
And the documentation's own permission to break outright, if that agreement is ever broken first.
